prompt: In this course's lab, what writes the replies that `pl check` counts?
hint: Read what the lab is made of.

choices.text: The person who labelled the test set, writing each reply by hand beside its message
choices.why: That person wrote the expected answers in `expect`, not the replies.

choices.text: `llama3.2:3b`, a small open model, run by Ollama on your computer
choices.why: Right. Every reply in a transcript was written by that model.

choices.text: A Python program written for the course that imitates a model by following fixed keyword rules
choices.why: Nothing in the lab imitates a model: the replies come from a real one.

choices.text: A commercial model reached with the course's API key
choices.why: The course hands out no key. The paid API is an option, with your own.

prompt: Why does the course recommend running the model on your own computer rather than through a paid API?
hint: Think about how many calls a lesson makes.

choices.text: Locally the many calls a lesson makes cost nothing and need no card
choices.why: Right, and no lesson then depends on a provider's free allowance.

choices.text: A local model answers better than any commercial one
choices.why: The section says the opposite: a commercial model is much stronger than `llama3.2:3b`.

choices.text: The harness cannot speak to an API over the internet
choices.why: It can: the section shows a `call()` for an OpenAI-compatible API.

choices.text: A local model gives the same reply on every computer, so the numbers in each lesson always match yours exactly
choices.why: Replies can differ between machines and versions; the section warns about exactly that.

prompt: A friend's computer has 4 GB of memory, and a one-line reply from `llama3.2:3b` takes over a minute. What does the lesson suggest?
hint: Two things were measured about the smaller model.

choices.text: Keep the 3b model and wait, because the smaller one changes nothing
choices.why: The smaller model needs less memory: 2.0 GB loaded against 2.9.

choices.text: Switch to `llama3.2:1b`, and expect lower counts
choices.why: Right: it passed 9 of 40 where the 3b model passed 28, and the checks work the same way.

choices.text: Run the 3b model in a virtual machine instead, which gives the model a larger and separate share of memory
choices.why: A virtual machine takes memory from the same computer and gets no graphics card.

choices.text: Raise `num_predict` so the reply is written in fewer steps
choices.why: `num_predict` caps how many tokens a reply may have; it does not make each one faster.

prompt: Which function in `pl.py` is the only one that knows the model is served by Ollama?
hint: The one you replace to use a paid API instead.

choices.text: `render()`
choices.why: `render()` fills placeholders; it never sends anything.

choices.text: `judge()`
choices.why: `judge()` reads a reply that already exists.

choices.text: `call()`
choices.why: Right. Everything else works on text and files.

choices.text: `cmd_run()`
choices.why: `cmd_run()` calls `call()` once per case; it does not know who answers.

prompt: A reply is not valid JSON. How many of the checks after `json` can it pass?

choices.text: All of them, if the content is right
choices.why: The harness cannot read fields out of text it could not parse.

choices.text: None: the first failure ends them
choices.why: Right. A reply that is not JSON has no fields to check.

choices.text: Only `category` and `urgency`, which read the content rather than the format
choices.why: Those read fields from the parsed object, and there is none.

choices.text: It depends on whether `--failures` is given
choices.why: `--failures` only lists the failures; it does not change the checks.

prompt: Why does `pl.py` set temperature 0 and a fixed seed by default?
hint: What should a difference between two runs mean?

choices.text: So that the model writes shorter replies
choices.why: Temperature and seed decide which tokens are chosen, not how many.

choices.text: So that a difference between two runs comes from the prompt
choices.why: Right, on one machine. Lesson 8 is about when to change them.

choices.text: So that every computer, whatever its processor and version of Ollama, prints exactly the numbers in the lessons
choices.why: Another machine or Ollama version can still word a reply differently.

choices.text: Because Ollama refuses a request without them
choices.why: Ollama has defaults of its own; the harness sets these on purpose.

prompt: `pl run` stops with `Connection refused`. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The model was never pulled
choices.why: A missing model gets an answer, a 404 naming the model; this got no answer at all.

choices.text: The Ollama server is not running
choices.why: Right. Start the service, or `ollama serve`, or the Ollama application.

choices.text: The test set has a line that is not JSON
choices.why: `pl` would fail reading the file, before it ever tried to connect.

choices.text: Python is older than 3.8 and cannot open a network connection
choices.why: An old Python fails with a syntax or import error, not a refused connection.

prompt: You pulled `llama3.2:3b` through the Linux service yesterday. Today, after starting `ollama serve` yourself, `ollama list` is empty. What happened?
hint: Where does a server look for its models?

choices.text: The model was deleted when the computer restarted
choices.why: Models are files on disk; a restart does not remove them.

choices.text: The download was incomplete, so Ollama discarded the partial files when it started again
choices.why: Then `ollama list` would not have shown it yesterday.

choices.text: Two servers: each reads models from the home of the user who started it
choices.why: Right: two servers, two model directories. Use the service, or pull again into yours.

choices.text: `ollama list` only shows models used in the last five minutes
choices.why: That is `ollama ps`, which shows what is loaded in memory.

prompt: On this machine the first reply took 34.8 seconds and the second 12.7, because the first call after the server starts has to ___ the model into memory.
hint: One word for what `ollama ps` then shows.

prompt: The bare prompt's reply to `t01` said `**Category:** Refund Request`. What was wrong with it?
hint: Read what the prompt asked for.

choices.text: Nothing: a person reads it happily, and a program that reads it can find the category and the urgency just as well
choices.why: A program needs JSON with known fields and known labels.

choices.text: The model misunderstood the customer
choices.why: The reply is a fair reading of the message.

choices.text: It is not JSON and the label is its own word: the prompt asked for neither
choices.why: Right: it is a gap in the prompt, filled with something plausible.

choices.text: The reply was cut off by `num_predict`
choices.why: `pl show` reports `stop: stop`, a reply that ended on its own.

prompt: Asking for JSON in words, how many of the forty replies passed every check?
Under `v2-json.txt` thirty-nine replies parsed. What was most of the remaining failures about?

choices.text: Text around the JSON, such as a code fence or a sentence before the object
choices.why: Only one reply failed to parse, and it was not wrapped.

choices.text: Labels: urgency or category
choices.why: Right, and seven of them were `normal` messages the model called `high`.

choices.text: Extra fields nobody asked for
choices.why: `fields` failed only where `json` had already failed.

choices.text: Replies cut off before the closing brace
choices.why: Every reply ended on its own.

prompt: `pl compare` reports `fixed 7, broken 1` between v2 and v3. Which messages carry evidence about whether the examples helped?
hint: The rest gave the same result both times.

choices.text: All forty
choices.why: A message that passed both times, or failed both times, says nothing about the change.

choices.text: The twenty-eight that pass under v3, since those are the ones the examples got right
choices.why: Most of those passed under v2 as well.

choices.text: The eight that changed
choices.why: Right: the sign test is computed on those eight.

choices.text: Only the one that broke
choices.why: The seven fixed ones are evidence too, in the other direction.

prompt: The test that asks how often a fair coin would split the changed results at least as unevenly is the ___ test.
hint: Its name is about which way each one moved.

prompt: The sign test gave p = 0.070 for seven fixed and one broken. What is the fair way to report the change?
hint: Five in a hundred is the usual bar.

choices.text: The examples are proved to help, since seven is far more than one
choices.why: Eight changes are few, and a fair coin splits them that unevenly seven times in a hundred.

choices.text: The examples made no difference at all, since the result is not significant at the usual bar of five in a hundred
choices.why: Not significant is not the same as no effect: the evidence points one way, weakly.

choices.text: Suggestive, not proof: more messages are needed
choices.why: Right. On forty messages a change needs more than seven fixes to carry itself.

choices.text: The test cannot be used, because the replies are deterministic
choices.why: The test is about the messages, not about sampling.

prompt: A study found few-shot gains survived even when the example labels were wrong. What does that suggest the examples were mostly teaching?

choices.text: The correct answer for each message
choices.why: Then wrong labels would have hurt much more.

choices.text: The answer's shape and its possible labels
choices.why: Right. That is the part an example shows and a description only says.

choices.text: Nothing: the gains were noise
choices.why: The gains were measured; the question is what produced them.

choices.text: That models ignore examples
choices.why: They did not ignore them; they learnt something other than the labels.

prompt: Why did adding examples move `t01`, a customer charged twice, from `high` to `normal`?

choices.text: The examples told the model to prefer `normal`
choices.why: No line says that; the pull came from what the examples are.

choices.text: The model became less careful with a longer prompt
choices.why: It answered every other billing message as before; the pull has a source.

choices.text: It resembles the first example, a billing refund that is `normal`
choices.why: Right: an example pulls the messages that look like it towards its labels.

choices.text: The message was mislabelled in the test set
choices.why: A double charge is urgent, and the model agreed until the examples arrived.

prompt: Which example teaches the model the most, for its tokens?

choices.text: An obvious case it would have got right anyway
choices.why: That one teaches the format and little else.

choices.text: A boundary case
choices.why: Right: that is where the model would otherwise guess.

choices.text: The longest message in the inbox
choices.why: Length is not what makes an example informative.

choices.text: A message copied from the test set, so that the example is known to be labelled correctly
choices.why: That one inflates the score by being answered by copying.

prompt: Why should an example never also be a test case?
hint: What does the model do with an example?

choices.text: It is answered by copying, inflating the score
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11 measures how far.

choices.text: The harness refuses to run a test set in which a case also appears as an example in the prompt
choices.why: `pl` checks no such thing.

choices.text: Test cases are longer than examples
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: An example has no `expect` field
choices.why: That is a detail of the file, not the reason.

prompt: `t01` went in as 108 tokens without the examples and 250 with them. How many tokens does every call now pay for the three examples and their tags?
Which of these are reasons the section gives for choosing examples carefully? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Every example pulls answers towards its own labels
choices.why: Yes: balance matters.

choices.text: Examples are paid for on every call
choices.why: Yes: they are part of every prompt.

choices.text: A model ignores examples after the third
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: Invented examples are cleaner than real messages
choices.why: Yes, and that is the problem: they teach nothing about messy input.

prompt: One example carried `"order": "4471"`. What happened to the forty replies?

choices.text: None of them changed
choices.why: `fields` failed five replies for a field nobody asked for.

choices.text: Every reply copied the field, whatever the message was about
choices.why: Thirty-five did not; the ones that did looked like the example.

choices.text: Five carried it, four wrongly
choices.why: Right: messages about an order or a payment, and four of them were given order 4471 wrongly.

choices.text: The model refused to answer
choices.why: Every reply came back.

prompt: Which check caught the copied order number, and why only that one?

choices.text: `json`, because the extra field broke the JSON
choices.why: The replies parsed: an extra field is still valid JSON.

choices.text: `fields`: it fails extra fields
choices.why: Right. A check that only looked for the fields it needed would have passed them.

choices.text: `labels`, because 4471 is not a label
choices.why: `labels` only reads `category` and `urgency`.

choices.text: `category`, because carrying an order number changed the category the model chose for each message
choices.why: The category was not what changed.

prompt: Why is a defect in an example easy to miss in a demo and loud in a test set?

choices.text: A demo uses a different model
choices.why: Same model, same prompt.

choices.text: It shows only in messages that resemble the example
choices.why: Right: `t04`, the login problem, came back clean.

choices.text: Test sets are checked by a person, who reads every reply and notices what a demo does not
choices.why: They are checked by `pl check`.

choices.text: The defect only appears at high temperature
choices.why: These runs were at temperature 0.

prompt: What does the section recommend to stop examples teaching the wrong thing? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Vary whatever should vary
choices.why: Yes: the model copies a pattern you did not mean.

choices.text: Remove names, order numbers, dates and amounts
choices.why: Yes: those turn up in other answers.

choices.text: Use as many examples as the prompt can hold
choices.why: Each one costs tokens on every call and pulls answers towards it.

choices.text: Check strictly, so a leak fails a test
choices.why: Yes: that is how the order number was caught.

prompt: Put the three prompts of this lesson in order of how many replies passed every check, fewest first.
items: The prompt that asks for JSON

prompt: Match each change to what it fixed or caused in this lesson.

pairs.left: Asking for JSON and listing the labels
pairs.right: The model's own field names and words

pairs.left: An order number left in one example
pairs.right: An extra field in five replies

right_distractors: Replies cut off in the middle

prompt: A colleague adds a fourth example and the score goes from 28 to 29 of 40. What would you want to see before keeping it?
hint: One more pass is one message.

choices.text: Nothing: any gain is worth keeping
choices.why: One message can move for reasons that have nothing to do with the example.

choices.text: Which messages changed, the sign test on them, and the token cost on every call
choices.why: Right: which messages changed, whether the change could be chance, and what it costs.

choices.text: A second run of the same prompt, to see whether 29 repeats or goes back to 28
choices.why: At temperature 0 it will repeat on that machine; that says nothing about the example.

choices.text: A longer prompt, to check the example is not too short
choices.why: Length is not the question.
